what: Profile of the Kotlin API under load, and an A/B of three small changes it suggested
hardware: Apple M3 Pro, 11 cores, 18 GiB; Docker Desktop VM with 11 CPUs and 11.67 GiB; k6 2.3.0 natively on the same Mac

profile.method: Java Flight Recorder inside the API container (JDK 17) during a 30 s run at 600/s, execution samples every 1 ms with 512-frame stacks; only samples inside the measured window counted (1,210). The raw recordings were not kept.
profile.result: No hotspot. The largest single frames were under 3% of samples each, spread over Ktor's request pipeline and coroutines, kotlinx JSON encoding and decoding, the PostgreSQL JDBC driver and the JDK HTTP client calling the scorer. Only about 5% of samples had an application frame on the stack, because most work runs in framework continuations and driver threads.

removable_items.regex matching (Pattern/Matcher frames): about 4% inclusive; precompiling removes compilation, not matching

change: Idempotency hash: HexFormat instead of String.format per byte; output unchanged (test against the FIPS 180-2 vector)
Validation regexes compiled once instead of on every request
Database.transaction no longer sets READ COMMITTED on every transaction; the pool already sets it once per connection, so PostgreSQL saves one SET statement per transaction
method: Same as bench/explain_ab_2026-10-22.json: fresh Compose project per run, 600/s, 15 s measured, cgroup CPU per completed authorization. Only the API image differed; order before, after, after, before, before, after. An unrelated PostgreSQL container from another project was idle on the machine throughout.
findings: No measurable difference: with b2 excluded, the before runs used 5.05 and 5.19 ms of stack CPU per authorization (API 1.38 and 1.47 ms) and the after runs 4.70-5.47 ms (API 1.26-1.52 ms); the ranges overlap.

Run b2 (before) was disturbed: 3,188 dropped iterations, 133 errors and p99 5 s, with every container's CPU per authorization about three times the others. The cause was not identified; it is reported and excluded.
Absolute CPU per authorization was lower on 23 October than in the 22 October runs of the same code (about 5.1 against 6.3 ms), so compare runs only within one A/B.

The API's cost is spread across framework, serialization, driver and HTTP-client work. In this workload cards carry only a velocity control, so the spend aggregates never run; an approved authorization makes ten SQL statements plus the commit. Joining the card and controls reads, or the holds and balance reads, would save at most two round trips, probably below this A/B's resolution.
limits: three runs per build with one excluded
one machine with k6 on it
